cash flow was −₹2,571 cr in H1 and net debt tripled in six months. At 12.1x our FY28E EPS the stock is at the top of its 14-year range

2. Growth is paid for in working capital
A distributor lends to its customers for ~59 days, holds stock for
~25 and borrows from vendors for ~45-50. Every ₹100 of extra
annual revenue needs roughly ₹10 of working capital. In H1 FY27
receivables rose ₹3,942 cr and inventory ₹3,673 cr, against payables
up ₹2,945 cr. Operating cash flow was −₹2,571 cr and borrowings
went from ₹2,637 cr to ₹5,992 cr. The CFO said free cash flow "may
not be a right metric" at this growth rate. Fair, but it is the metric
that decides whether growth creates value.
3. Spread, not growth, drives the value
At a 2.25% EBITDA margin and 37 year-end working-capital days,
the core business earns a post-tax return on capital of about 16%.
The stock's measured risk puts our WACC at 13.7% (2-year beta
1.60, Blume-adjusted 1.40). The spread is narrow, so extra revenue

The growth is on the balance sheet
Balance-sheet days use annualised Q4 FY26 / Q2 FY27 revenue; the company's own
figure is 35 days for Q2 FY27 (we compute 35). Leases: ₹371 cr.
H1 FY27 was the best half on record for profit and, in the data we
have (FY23 onward), the worst for cash. Inventory rose 45% in six
months while quarterly revenue rose 29%. Management blamed
Middle East supply-chain stress: the Strait of Hormuz closure
pushed purchases that used to arrive ~85% by sea onto air freight
and longer routes. It also cited distributors stocking up to secure
supply as prices rose. Middle East vendors extended extra credit.
That helped, but it can be withdrawn.

An emerging-markets distributor with a small, troubled Turkish arm
Redington distributes IT, mobility, software and solar products in
~40 markets: India and South Asia (SISA, 60% of Q2 revenue), the
Middle East, Africa, Turkey and Central Asia (ROW). It carries ~460
brands and sells through 76,000 channel partners. It is the #1
distributor in India and the Middle East and among the ten largest
IT distributors worldwide, despite having no presence in the US,
Europe or China. It has no promoter. Taiwan's Synnex Technology
The economics are thin margins on fast-turning capital: gross
margin ~5%, EBITDA ~2%, working capital ~35 days, giving a pre-
tax ROCE of ~20-23%. Over FY07-FY26 revenue compounded at 15%
a year. EBITDA margin peaked at 3.0% (FY12) and has drifted to ~2%
as mobility and large deals grew.
Investor data book (29-Jun-26) and decks. The corporate deck shows different
ROCE history (e.g. FY24 22.5%); we use the data book. Year-end WC days are our
SISA is the engine: Q2 revenue +66%, PAT +66%, ROCE 28.8%, ROE
29.5%. Middle East and Africa revenue still grew 41% despite the
West Asia conflict that began on 28-Feb-26. UAE and Saudi Arabia
were flat to slightly down in Q1, while the rest of the GCC and
Levant (+121% in Q2) and Africa (+35%) grew fast. War-risk freight
and insurance cost ~$3 mn in Q1, only partly passed on.
Arena: why the minority stake is now a liability
Arena Bilgisayar (Borsa Istanbul) was bought in 2012 for Turkish IT
distribution. Since then it has sold Paynet (FY25), exited the
Vodafone contract and its lira-denominated working-capital
business, and seen revenue halve. With 35-40% local inflation and
a "hypercompetitive" market, the remaining dollar business loses
money: Redington's share was −₹122 cr in FY26 and −₹107 cr in H1
FY27, and Q2 added a ₹135 cr bad-debt provision. The trade-name
intangible (US$25.6 mn) has now been fully written off (₹152 cr Q4
FY26, ₹80 cr Q2 FY27). Management is "trying to see strategically
what we should do" (Q1 call) and on 4-Nov declined to give a
timeline. Arena's listed equity is worth ~TRY 1.15 bn (~₹220 cr) at
100%, about ₹1.4/share for Redington's half, so selling it would
not move the value needle. Stopping the losses would: ₹1.5-2.7 of

Why a 21.6% ROE does not rescue the valuation
Reported ROE has climbed to a record 21.6% and now exceeds our
15.0% cost of equity. But ~25-30% of working capital is debt-
funded, so ROE is levered ROIC. The equity's measured beta of 1.60
is the price of that leverage. The test for value creation is ROIC
(~16% post-tax in our Base) against WACC (13.7%): a positive
spread, but a narrow one. That is why the DCF is only modestly
